planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Black Knight is a purple passionfruit selection prized for its unusually dark, near-black rind and rich, intensely flavored pulp.

directions: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Black Knight is a purple passionfruit cultivar distinguished by its deep, nearly black rind at full ripeness and dense, richly aromatic, sweet-tart pulp that many growers rate among the most flavorful of the purple types. Like other purple passionfruit, it fruits within the first year from a rooted cutting or grafted plant and drops ripe fruit naturally from the vine when ready to pick. The vine is vigorous and needs sturdy support along with periodic tip-pruning to keep growth directed toward fruiting wood. In zone 9, site it in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and mulch the root zone heavily before winter, since it shares the cold sensitivity typical of purple passionfruit types and can be damaged or killed by a hard freeze.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Passionfruit Production

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants at the base of a sturdy trellis or fence after the last frost; Panama Gold is the yellow-fruited counterpart to Panama Red, selected for large fruit size and vigorous production.

directions: Train onto a strong trellis or fence in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Panama Gold is a yellow-skinned passionfruit selection bred alongside Panama Red, producing notably large, thick-rinded fruit with abundant, tart-aromatic golden pulp well suited to juicing as well as fresh eating. The vine is vigorous and heavy-bearing, climbing quickly and beginning to fruit within its first year from a rooted cutting or grafted plant. Unlike many yellow (flavicarpa-type) passionfruit, which generally require cross-pollination between genetically distinct vines, growers should plant two Panama Gold vines or interplant with another compatible passionfruit to ensure reliable fruit set. Provide sturdy support and regular tip-pruning, and mulch the root zone heavily going into winter in zone 9, since this cultivar remains sensitive to hard freezes.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Passion Fruit Growing in the Home Garden
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Passionfruit Production

common_name: Honey Babe Peach (Genetic Dwarf Container Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Honey Babe is a genetic dwarf reaching only about 4–5 feet tall, one of the most compact true dwarf peaches available for containers or very small gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container of at least 15 gallons; Honey Babe is a genetic dwarf peach bred by Floyd Zaiger that naturally stays around 4–5 feet tall rather than being size-controlled by rootstock, yet still bears full-sized, richly flavored yellow freestone fruit that many home growers rate among the sweetest of the dwarf peach types. Its compact, densely branched form and showy pink spring blossoms make it as ornamental as it is productive, and it is self-fruitful, requiring no second pollinator tree. Thin developing fruit to about 4–6 inches apart once set, since the small tree can easily overbear relative to its size, and prune lightly each dormant season to maintain an open, sunlit canopy.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — genetic dwarf stone fruit variety notes

common_name: Southern Flame Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Container Nectarine)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Southern Flame is a genetic dwarf reaching only about 5–6 feet tall, from the same breeding lineage as El Dorado and Necta Zee.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, in the ground or in a large container, and thin fruit to 4–6 inches apart once marble-sized, since this naturally compact tree can overset relative to its small stature. Southern Flame is a genetic dwarf nectarine, part of the same Zaiger-bred family of true dwarf stone fruit as El Dorado and Necta Zee, growing only about 5–6 feet tall while still producing full-sized, freestone fruit with red-blushed yellow skin and sweet, richly flavored yellow flesh in mid-to-late summer. It is self-fruitful and needs no separate pollinator, and its dense, naturally rounded form suits a patio container or small garden bed where a standard nectarine tree would be impractical. As with other nectarines, watch for leaf curl and brown rot in humid Gulf Coast conditions and prune lightly each winter to keep the canopy open.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery — genetic dwarf stone fruit variety notes
